sources.title: ANU Press: Malayic Dayak and a Bornean homeland of Malay
sources.note: University synthesis links conservative Bornean Malayic languages to Proto-Malayic and seventh-century Old Malay while preserving scholarly uncertainty.

sources.title: Cambridge Handbook: geographic and demographic expansion of Malay
sources.note: Authoritative linguistic chapter distinguishes Old Malay, later trade languages, regional varieties, and the evidence behind mapped expansion.

sources.title: UNESCO Silk Roads: Ancient trading centres in the Malay Peninsula
sources.note: Authoritative archaeological synthesis covers early port discovery, coastal exchange, Chinese ceramics, craft finds, and changing interpretations.

sources.title: National Museum of the Philippines: Ginikanan/Gigikanan
sources.note: National museum exhibition presents Butuan as a distinct maritime transit port and trading center within wider Southeast Asian exchange.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Muarajambi Temple Compound
sources.note: Official heritage dossier situates Malayu and Srivijaya in trade, Buddhist learning, architecture, and the seventh-to-fourteenth-century Batanghari landscape.

sources.title: ANU: Prehistory of the Indo-Malaysian Archipelago
sources.note: University monograph synthesizes archaeology and language evidence across the archipelago while warning against simple ethnic readings of material culture.

sources.title: ANU: Notes on the prehistory and internal subgrouping of Malayic
sources.note: Comparative linguistic study places the likely Proto-Malayic homeland near western Borneo and explains uncertainty in subgroup reconstruction.

sources.title: ANU record: Archaeological correlations for Malayo-Polynesian dispersal
sources.note: Oxford handbook chapter record frames more than eight hundred Malayo-Polynesian languages and separates archaeological, genetic, and linguistic arguments.

sources.title: Antiquity: rice, beans, and trade crops on the early maritime route
sources.note: Peer-reviewed archaeobotany dates Khao Sam Kaeo and Phu Khao Thong and identifies rice, millets, pulses, cotton, sesame, and mixed communities.

sources.title: Cambridge Archaeological Journal: Southeast Asian port networks
sources.note: Peer-reviewed synthesis identifies specialized glass and stone industries, settlement networks, and fourth-to-first-century BCE port chronology.

sources.title: Cambridge: Indian and Indian-style wares from Khao Sam Kaeo
sources.note: Scholarly technological study uses fourth-to-second-century BCE ceramics to examine local production, exchange, and interaction with South Asia.

sources.title: UNESCO Silk Roads PDF: Ancient ports in Malaysia
sources.note: Full archaeological report documents Kuala Selinsing food remains, deep-sea fish, shell, burials, a child grave, pottery, beads, and nonviolent abandonment.

sources.title: UNESCO Silk Roads: Kuala Selinsing and Pulau Kelumpang preservation
sources.note: Authoritative article summarizes the long occupation sequence and oxygen-poor mangrove preservation of food, burials, pottery, gems, and jewelry.

sources.title: British Museum: Bukit Tengku Lembu cemetery collection
sources.note: Museum catalogue dates excavated bowls, stands, urns, and tazzas from a Perlis cemetery to roughly 300 to 200 BCE.

sources.title: British Museum: second-century BCE bell from Selangor
sources.note: Museum catalogue preserves a firmly catalogued second-century BCE metal object from the peninsula without assigning its maker an ethnicity.

sources.title: Department of Museums Malaysia: Lembah Bujang Archaeological Museum
sources.note: National museum describes third-to-twelfth-century port trade, ceramics, glass beads, architecture, and Hindu-Buddhist material at Bujang Valley.

sources.title: Indonesian Cultural Preservation Agency: Kedukan Bukit inscription
sources.note: Government heritage record supplies the 682 Old Malay inscription text, dates, voyage, troops, boats, settlement, and prosperity formula.

sources.title: Indonesian Cultural Preservation Agency: Telaga Batu inscription
sources.note: Government heritage record dates the Old Malay-Pallava inscription and lists royal relatives, officials, scribes, smiths, captains, merchants, washers, servants, and loyalty rituals.

sources.title: Indonesian Heritage Directorate: resin in Srivijaya trade
sources.note: Government archaeology traces damar from inland river collection sites through traders and ship captains to Palembang and overseas exchange.

sources.title: Cambridge: rise of the Srivijayan thalassocracy
sources.note: University history distinguishes Malayu at Jambi from Srivijaya, Chinese records, Old Malay inscriptions, and shifting maritime power.

sources.title: Cambridge: Esoteric Buddhism in Mediaeval Maritime Asia
sources.note: Scholarly volume documents Yijing learning Sanskrit at Srivijaya in 671 and the port-capital as an international Buddhist center.

sources.title: Nalanda University: Searching for the Curriculum of Sriwijaya
sources.note: University study links Balaputradeva of Suvarnadvipa with a ninth-century Nalanda monastery and examines transregional education evidence.

sources.title: National Museum of the Philippines: Laguna inscription and Butuan boats
sources.note: National museum dates the Laguna Copperplate to 900, identifies Early Kawi writing, and places it beside regional boat and ceramic evidence.

sources.title: Philippine Studies: Laguna Copperplate inscription text and translation
sources.note: Peer-reviewed edition gives the ten-line Old Malay-dominant text, Early Kawi transliteration, debt release, people, titles, and places.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Butuan Archaeological Sites
sources.note: National Museum nomination documents tenth-to-thirteenth-century boats, trade ceramics, gold workshops, burials, and international port activity.

sources.title: National Museum of the Philippines: Butuan regional museum
sources.note: National museum records boat excavations, waterlogged context, eighth-to-tenth-century dating, and preserved material culture.

sources.title: Sarawak Museum Department: archaeology at Santubong
sources.note: State museum identifies Santubong as a major eleventh-to-thirteenth-century trading and iron-working center with thousands of ceramic sherds.

sources.title: Indonesian Heritage Directorate: Candi Astano at Muarojambi
sources.note: Government archaeology documents a temple enclosure, surrounding ditch, Song-Yuan ceramics, beads, hearth remains, and a temporary pilgrim settlement.

sources.title: Brill: Political economy and trade in pre-Islamic South Sulawesi
sources.note: Archaeological synthesis dates widespread Chinese and mainland Southeast Asian trade wares from about the thirteenth century and separates later Bugis kingdoms.

sources.title: Indonesian Cultural Preservation Agency: temples of West Sumatra
sources.note: Government heritage synthesis places Malayu first near Jambi and later Dharmasraya, with the dated 1286 Amoghapasa inscription.

sources.title: BRIN archaeology journal: Periodization of Candi Simangambat
sources.note: Government archaeology dates the 1275 Pamalayu expedition and the 1286 Amoghapasa diplomatic gift sent to Malayu.

sources.title: UNESCO Memory of the World: Terengganu Inscribed Stone
sources.note: Authoritative heritage record identifies the earliest Jawi evidence in the Malay Muslim world; its nomination dates the Malay text to 1303.

sources.title: UNESCO Memory of the World nomination: Terengganu Inscribed Stone
sources.note: Official nomination describes the Malay Jawi inscription, 702 Hijri date corresponding to 1303, law, trade, and cultural setting.

sources.title: Malaysia National Heritage Department: Terengganu Inscribed Stone
sources.note: Government heritage account identifies early Jawi, regional maritime commerce, religious law, Sanskrit survivals, and continuity of earlier life.

sources.title: Indonesian archaeology: sago and the Talang Tuo garden
sources.note: Government-hosted archaeological study links the 684 garden inscription with coconut, areca, sugar palm, sago, bamboo, and edible fruit.

sources.title: Indonesian Heritage Directorate: Kota Kapur site
sources.note: Government archaeology documents a seventh-century Old Malay inscription, stone-laterite structure, religious sculpture, and Bangka setting.

sources.title: Cambridge: Ships, Sailors and Kingdoms of Ancient Southeast Asia
sources.note: Scholarly maritime history covers seafaring technology, exchange, and political diversity from 500 BCE to 1500 CE.

sources.title: Cambridge: Commodity flows in the eastern Indian Ocean, 1000 to 1500
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study emphasizes merchant agency, diasporas, commodities, port competition, Chola raids, and porous political boundaries.

sources.title: National Museum of the Philippines: pre-colonial burial traditions
sources.note: National museum survey distinguishes regional burial practices and dates boat-shaped coffins at several Philippine sites to the twelfth through fifteenth centuries.

sources.title: Department of Museums Malaysia: Kedah epigraphy workshop
sources.note: National museum publication lists Bujang Valley inscriptions and distinguishes Sanskrit-Pallava records from later Old Malay forms.

sources.title: Malaysia National Heritage Department: Malay manuscripts
sources.note: Government heritage overview discusses writing materials and makes clear that surviving Malay manuscript culture is substantially later than the target windows.

proposedOverrides.name: Malay
proposedOverrides.summary: Three atlas labels connect many distinct maritime societies.

claims.locator: University synthesis links conservative Bornean Malayic languages to Proto-Malayic and seventh-century Old Malay while preserving scholarly uncertainty. Authoritative linguistic chapter distinguishes Old Malay, later trade languages, regional varieties, and the evidence behind mapped expansion. Authoritative archaeological synthesis covers early port discovery, coastal exchange, Chinese ceramics, craft finds, and changing interpretations. National museum exhibition presents Butuan as a distinct maritime transit port and trading center within wider Southeast Asian exchange. Official heritage dossier situates Malayu and Srivijaya in trade, Buddhist learning, architecture, and the seventh-to-fourteenth-century Batanghari landscape.
claims.uncertainty: Scope and distinctions are explicit in the card; no polygon accuracy is inferred.

claims.locator: Pre-start control for the earliest label and representative island point ownership. Sole snapshot containing malays; decoded fourteen-component geometry, point membership, arcs, and source hash. Peer-reviewed synthesis identifies specialized glass and stone industries, settlement networks, and fourth-to-first-century BCE port chronology.
claims.uncertainty: Approximate interpretive phase; see the attributed dating discussion.

claims.locator: Endpoint control where the early label disappears without a documented population-ending event. Full archaeological report documents Kuala Selinsing food remains, deep-sea fish, shell, burials, a child grave, pottery, beads, and nonviolent abandonment.
claims.uncertainty: Approximate interpretive phase; see the attributed dating discussion.

claims.locator: Scholarly technological study uses fourth-to-second-century BCE ceramics to examine local production, exchange, and interaction with South Asia. Scholarly maritime history covers seafaring technology, exchange, and political diversity from 500 BCE to 1500 CE.
claims.uncertainty: Approximate interpretive phase; see the attributed dating discussion.

claims.locator: Government archaeology documents a seventh-century Old Malay inscription, stone-laterite structure, religious sculpture, and Bangka setting. National museum publication lists Bujang Valley inscriptions and distinguishes Sanskrit-Pallava records from later Old Malay forms.
claims.uncertainty: Approximate interpretive phase; see the attributed dating discussion.

claims.locator: Government heritage record supplies the 682 Old Malay inscription text, dates, voyage, troops, boats, settlement, and prosperity formula. University history distinguishes Malayu at Jambi from Srivijaya, Chinese records, Old Malay inscriptions, and shifting maritime power.
claims.uncertainty: Approximate interpretive phase; see the attributed dating discussion.

claims.locator: Pre-start control for the medieval malay record and its neighboring atlas categories. Scholarly volume documents Yijing learning Sanskrit at Srivijaya in 671 and the port-capital as an international Buddhist center.
claims.uncertainty: Approximate interpretive phase; see the attributed dating discussion.

claims.locator: First medieval malay snapshot; decoded eleven-component geometry and direct topology seams with Srivijaya and Mataram. National museum describes third-to-twelfth-century port trade, ceramics, glass beads, architecture, and Hindu-Buddhist material at Bujang Valley.
claims.uncertainty: Approximate interpretive phase; see the attributed dating discussion.

claims.locator: Second medieval malay snapshot; unchanged target geometry but changed surrounding owner layers. National museum dates the Laguna Copperplate to 900, identifies Early Kawi writing, and places it beside regional boat and ceramic evidence.
claims.uncertainty: Approximate interpretive phase; see the attributed dating discussion.

claims.locator: Endpoint control where malay disappears while island communities and documented ports continue. Peer-reviewed study emphasizes merchant agency, diasporas, commodities, port competition, Chola raids, and porous political boundaries.
claims.uncertainty: Approximate interpretive phase; see the attributed dating discussion.

claims.locator: Pre-start control for the late malays-1200 label and regional political layers. State museum identifies Santubong as a major eleventh-to-thirteenth-century trading and iron-working center with thousands of ceramic sherds.
claims.uncertainty: Approximate interpretive phase; see the attributed dating discussion.

claims.locator: Sole malays-1200 snapshot; decoded three-component Borneo, Sulawesi, and Mindanao-Sulu envelope with topology seams. Archaeological synthesis dates widespread Chinese and mainland Southeast Asian trade wares from about the thirteenth century and separates later Bugis kingdoms.
claims.uncertainty: Approximate interpretive phase; see the attributed dating discussion.

claims.locator: Government archaeology dates the 1275 Pamalayu expedition and the 1286 Amoghapasa diplomatic gift sent to Malayu. Official nomination describes the Malay Jawi inscription, 702 Hijri date corresponding to 1303, law, trade, and cultural setting.
claims.uncertainty: Approximate interpretive phase; see the attributed dating discussion.
